takeaway: Hierarchical Prefetching marks large call-graph Bundles in software, then hardware records and replays each Bundle’s recent instruction footprint across local control-flow variation.
background: Server software spans application logic, libraries, runtimes, and kernels, producing instruction working sets larger than processor caches. Instruction prefetchers try to fetch code before the front end stalls.
villain: Existing fetch-directed and history-based prefetchers either look too little ahead to hide long miss latency or lose accuracy when runtime control flow diverges from recorded fine-grained paths.
approach: A link-time call-graph analysis finds major divergence points and records Bundle entry points in the binary for the loader to tag. When a tagged entry commits, hardware non-speculatively selects that Bundle, records retired instruction blocks, and replays its most recent compressed footprint into the instruction cache in paced segments. Most footprint metadata stays in main memory, while a small on-chip table locates each Bundle’s record.
impact: The authors claim that coarse-grained functional context lets an instruction prefetcher run farther ahead with less on-chip metadata than the evaluated fine-grained alternatives.

evaluation.overview: The authors use full-system gem5 simulation to measure IPC, prefetch timeliness, coverage, accuracy, cache-level latency, sensitivity, Bundle behavior, and memory-bandwidth overhead on server applications.
evaluation.implemented: A released gem5 implementation of the software analysis, binary tagging interface, Compression Buffer, on-chip Metadata Address Table, and record/replay engine with a per-core in-memory Metadata Buffer.
evaluation.setting: The simulation models a 4 GHz Sunny-Cove-like x86-64 out-of-order CPU running Ubuntu, with a 32 KB L1 instruction cache, 512 KB private L2, and 2 MB-per-core shared LLC allocation. Eleven web, database, ORM, and OLTP workloads warm for 100 million instructions and measure the next 100 million.

results.text: Across the eleven simulated server workloads, the authors report a 6.6% average IPC improvement over FDIP; EIP, the strongest evaluated prior prefetcher, improves IPC by 4.0%.
The authors report that Hierarchical Prefetching reduced average instruction demand-miss latency by 38.7% beyond FDIP, compared with 19.7% for EIP.

limitations: All performance evidence is from gem5 rather than a processor prototype. The design assumes link/load-time call-graph analysis can tag Bundle entries, successive Bundle executions have similar instruction-block footprints, and the ISA offers reserved tag bits or can add a marker instruction; it also reserves a 512 KB per-core metadata buffer in memory.
phd_group_signal: The work signals a microarchitecture style that begins with workload control-flow measurements, divides responsibility across the binary toolchain and hardware, and tests mechanisms through full-system simulation and sensitivity studies.

claims.text: Software partitions a static call graph into Bundles and exposes their entry points; hardware then records each Bundle’s dynamic retired-instruction footprint and replays the latest record in paced segments after a tagged entry commits.

The mechanism relies on stable repeated Bundle footprints, link/load-time access to the application and dynamically linked code, an instruction-tagging interface, and simulated main-memory storage for most prefetch metadata.
